item.title: China’s Downstream Nations Need a Collective Voice
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

China is building the world’s largest hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet, designed with a massive 60,000-megawatt capacity. Construction was formally launched in July 2025, much to the consternation of people across the border in India.

“China has already begun construction of a dam in Medog County, around 40 km from the border… without consulting us or sharing any information,” warned Chief Minister Pema Khandu of Arunachal Pradesh. He called China’s $167 billion mega-dam in a seismically active zone an existential potential “water bomb.”

The Medog dam is not an isolated incident. It’s just one sign of a larger crisis extending across Asia’s river basins, where downstream nations face upper-riparian infrastructure that proceeds unilaterally, without environmental impact disclosures, binding legal frameworks, or genuine transboundary consultation and governance.

Downstream states urgently need a collective voice, built on shared demands for data and transparency.

Known as the “Water Tower of Asia,” Tibet is the source of 10 major transboundary river systems that flow into 10 downstream nations. These vital waterways sustain ecosystems, agriculture, and the livelihoods of 1.8 billion people across South and Southeast Asia, nearly one-quarter of the global population. No other single territory matches this human impact in supplying transboundary freshwater to densely populated downstream nations. That gives Tibet an unparalleled position in global hydrology.

Tibet also stores more freshwater than any place on earth apart from the two poles, which is why it is often referred to as the Third Pole of the planet. However, Tibet faces a dual crisis: it is warming at roughly twice the global average while its high-altitude environment is also continually battered by mining, deforestation, and industrial activity – a combination that threatens the stability of Asia’s major rivers.

Tibet’s glaciers, permafrost, wetlands, lakes, and high-altitude ecosystems regulate water availability and influence downstream hydrological and ecological processes. Large-scale damming on these rivers, much of it is in highly seismic terrain and without transparency or treaty frameworks, deepens downstream uncertainty over water flows and flooding risks that cross borders.

China rejects these concerns outright. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun stated that China has carried out cooperation with downstream countries and has had necessary communication with them. The spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in India, Yu Jing, insisted that the dam project on the Yarlung Tsangpo will not have a negative impact on the ecological environment, geological conditions, and the rights and interests related to water resources of downstream countries. Rather, she claimed that it will “to some extent, help with their disaster prevention and reduction and climate response.”

However, downstream nations have deep concern about the absence of binding agreements. China voted against the 1997 U.N. Watercourses Convention and has no binding water-sharing treaty with its neighbors, while the non-binding memoranda that once underpinned data-sharing have lapsed. Many analysts therefore fear that China could weaponize Tibet’s water and assume the role of “Asia’s water hegemon,” driven largely by its favorable geopolitical position.

As China controls the headwaters of three major Indian river systems – the Brahmaputra, Indus, and Sutlej – opaque upstream water governance has become an acute national security concern for India. China has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to weaponize water transparency. During the Doklam standoff in 2017, China abruptly halted providing crucial monsoon-season water-flow data for the Yarlung Tsangpo (which becomes the Brahmaputra in India), citing station upgrades, an explanation many Indian analysts doubted as it was sharing the same data with Bangladesh. Cooperation has since eroded further, with the expiration of bilateral data-sharing agreements on the Sutlej in 2020 and the Brahmaputra in 2023.

Now, China is building the world’s largest mega-dam on a seismically volatile fault roughly 40 kilometers from the Indian border, risking catastrophic flooding across Arunachal Pradesh and Assam and endangering millions of lives. The 2000 Yigong dam breach in Tibet showed how violently upstream surges can hit downstream countries – the ensuing flood displaced 50,000 people across Arunachal Pradesh and Assam.

In 2024, 10-Point Call from Tibetan Experts in India demanded full environmental transparency for the downstream nations, immediate halt to large hydropower projects lacking local consent, and adhere to Free, Prior, and Informed Consent to prevent forced relocations and cultural destruction in Tibet.

India is not alone in expressing concerns about China’s unilateral approach to water issues. It’s also a recurring point of frustration for Southeast Asian countries on the Mekong River, known as the Lancang in China.

In 2016, a severe drought hit the Mekong Delta in Vietnam. The Stimson Center later published satellite-based evidence that upstream dam operations in China restricted river flow even when the upper basin recorded above-average rain and snowmelt. During this upstream squeeze, 166,000 hectares of rice-growing land was rendered infertile, leaving 2 million people without adequate drinking water. The Vietnam’s Ministry of Agriculture estimated that $4 billion was required to combat the drought and salinization in the Delta region.

Mekong River Commission (MRC) projections warn that cumulative damming could cut total delta sediment by up to 97 percent by 2040. Moreover, according to the World Wildlife Fund, the Mekong Giant Catfish stocks declined by 90 percent over the past two decades – a warning that could slash the world’s fourth largest fishing industry.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-20 13:59 UTC

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/chinas-downstream-nations-need-a-collective-voice/
